Executive summary

This note does not cover the situation in the Russian-occupied regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

LGBT+ people in Georgia are unlikely to face a real risk of persecution or serious harm from the state. The onus is on the person to demonstrate otherwise.

The Constitution of Georgia stipulates that all persons are equal before the law and prohibits any form of discrimination although it does not explicitly prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity or expression. A person’s sex or sexual orientation is formally recognised as a protected ground under anti-discrimination legislation and as a basis of intolerance constituting an aggravating circumstance under the Criminal Code but rarely treated as such in practice. Similar references to gender identity were removed from several laws in 2025.

The 2024 Law on the Protection of Family Values and Minors introduced a range of restrictions affecting LGBT+ people, including prohibitions of same-sex marriages, gender-affirming health care, legal gender reassignment or recognition measures, adoption, and fostering. The law further prohibits ‘popularisation’ of same-sex relationships and gender identities. While there were no documented cases of punishments imposed for violating the law, civil society organisations report self-censorship in media output on LGBT+ issues, advocacy, and awareness campaigns.

Entrenched stereotypes and prejudice against persons of diverse SOGIE continue to exist in Georgian society. LGBT+ people face systemic barriers to healthcare, employment, and education. Trans, gender-diverse, and intersex individuals are particularly affected by the 2024 ban of gender-affirming health care. Trans people also face greater exclusion from the labour market.

Spaces for the LGBT+ community to gather are limited and largely concentrated in Tbilisi. While support organisations exist, they face challenges such as vandalism of offices and staff homes and difficult fund-raising procedures following the recent adoption of foreign agent legislation. No Pride events or demonstrations were documented since 2024. Representatives of the ruling Georgian Dream party as well as pro-government media platforms frequently engage in homo- and transphobic rhetoric and portray LGBT+ activism as ‘propaganda’.

A person who has a well-founded fear of persecution or serious harm from a non-state actor is unlikely to be able to obtain protection from the state, as the state is, in general, able but not willing to provide effective protection.

Official statistics on the investigation, prosecution, and conviction for SOGIE-related hate crimes show a decreasing trend, with no hate crimes based on gender identity recorded in 2025. According to civil society and the media, however, violent hate crimes against the LGBT+ community have become more frequent in recent years and are underreported in official statistics. As such, Georgia’s criminal justice system is not considered to be effectively addressing anti-LGBT+ hate crimes. The Public Defender and human rights protection mechanisms are reportedly also not actively investigating complaints by LGBT+ individuals.

In general, internal relocation is likely to be reasonable and not unduly harsh, particularly to urban areas and large cities, such as Tbilisi.

Each case must be considered on its individual facts. Where a claim is refused, it is unlikely to be certifiable as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

Assessment

Section updated: 17 September 2026

About the assessment

This section considers relevant evidence – including country information, refugee and human rights law and policy, and case law – to assess whether, in general:

a person faces a real risk of persecution or serious harm by state or non-state actors because of their actual or perceived sexual orientation and/or gender identity or expression

the state (or quasi state bodies) can provide effective protection

internal relocation is possible to avoid persecution or serious harm

if refused, a claim is likely or not to be certified as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

This note assesses the situation of actual and perceived lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans and people of other minority sexual orientations and gender identities (LGBT+). Sources often refer to LGBT+ people collectively, but the experiences of each group may differ. Where information is available, the note will refer to and consider the treatment of each group discretely. This note does not cover the situation in the Russian-occupied regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

Each case must be considered on its individual facts.

For details on how CPIT makes its assessments, gathers and presents country information, its research methodology and disclaimers and explainers on coverage, source selection, maps, translations and the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in developing CPIT products, see About country policy and information notes.

1. Material facts, credibility and other checks

1.1.1 Decision makers must:

assess credibility (see the Asylum Instructions on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status, on Sexual identity issues in the asylum claim, and Gender identity issues in the asylum claim.)

check if there has been a previous application for a UK visa or another form of leave. Asylum applications matched to visas should be investigated prior to the asylum interview (see the Asylum Instruction on Visa Matches, Asylum Claims from UK Visa Applicants).

consider making an international biometric data-sharing check, when one has not already been undertaken (see Biometric data-sharing process (Migration 5 biometric data-sharing process)).

consider language analysis testing, where available, in cases where there are doubts surrounding a person’s claimed place of origin (see the Asylum Instruction on Language Analysis)

3. Convention reason(s)

3.1.1 Actual or imputed particular social group (PSG).

3.1.2 LGBT+ people form a PSG in Georgia within the meaning of the Refugee Convention because they share an innate characteristic or a common background that cannot be changed, or share a characteristic or belief that is so fundamental to identity or conscience that a person should not be forced to renounce it and have a distinct identity in Georgia because the group is perceived as being different by the surrounding society.

3.1.3 Although people of diverse SOGIE in Georgia form a PSG, establishing such membership is not sufficient to be recognised as a refugee. The question to be addressed is whether the person has a well-founded fear of persecution on account of their membership of such a group.

3.1.4 For further guidance on the 5 Refugee Convention grounds, see the Asylum Instructions on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status.

4. Risk

4.1 Risk from the state

4.1.1 LGBT+ people in Georgia are, in general, unlikely to face a real risk of persecution or serious harm from the state. The onus is on the person to demonstrate otherwise.

4.1.2 Consensual same-sex sexual acts are not prohibited (see Provisions relating to same-sex relationships, marriage, and civil union).

4.1.3 The Constitution of Georgia stipulates that all persons are equal before the law and prohibits any form of discrimination, although it does not explicitly prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity or expression. Other laws contain non-discrimination provisions relating to sex or sexual orientation. In 2025, laws that had explicitly protected gender identity were amended. While protections based on sexual orientation remain in place, gender identity and gender expression were removed as protected characteristics under anti-discrimination legislation and intolerance on the ground of gender or gender identity is no longer considered an aggravating circumstance under the Criminal Code, a provision that had rarely been enforced previously (see Anti-discrimination provisions and New state policy and legislation affecting LGBT+ people).

4.1.4 The Law on the Protection of Family Values and Minors, adopted in 2024, introduced a range of restrictions affecting LGBT+ people. The law prohibits ‘popularisation’, defined as the dissemination of information that may be regarded as promoting or presenting same-sex relationships, diverse sexual orientations or gender identities in a positive light. Restrictions apply to media, educational materials, demonstrations and assemblies, as well as other forms of public communication. ‘Popularisation’ in education and advertising is punishable through fines set out in the Administrative Offences Code of Georgia. The legislation defines ‘popularisation’ broadly, leaving scope for varying interpretations as to what expressions are prohibited. Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) report self-censorship in media output on LGBT+ issues, advocacy, and public awareness campaigns on sex education to avoid potential prosecution of staff (see Provisions relating to awareness-raising and activism, Support organisations and New state policy and legislation affecting LGBT+ people).

4.1.5 The 2024 Law on the Protection of Family Values and Minors furthermore prohibits legal recognition of same-sex unions as marriage, including where people have married abroad. Its definition of marriage as a union of a woman and a man for the purpose of founding a family had previously been introduced by a 2017 amendment to the Georgian constitution (see Provisions relating to same-sex relationships, marriage, and civil union).

4.1.6 The 2024 Law on the Protection of Family Values and Minors also restricts adoption and fostering to heterosexual individuals. Prior to the adoption of the 2024 law, Georgian law did not expressly prohibit adoption by LGBT+ people and single individuals were able to adopt, subject to statutory requirements. As Georgian law did not recognise same-sex marriages or civil unions, same-sex couples did not have a legal avenue to adopt jointly as a couple (see Provisions relating to same-sex relationships, marriage, and civil union).

4.1.7 The 2024 Law on the Protection of Family Values and Minors prohibits gender-transition procedures and legal measures associated with gender reassignment or legal gender recognition. Previously, the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) had held in its 2022 judgment in the case of A.D. and Others v. Georgia that ‘it is not clear at all what the legal regime for the change of the sex/gender marker [in civil-status records] actually is in Georgia’ (paragraph 74). Notably, the ECtHR had found in the same judgment that ‘despite the fact that … a right [to change the sex/gender marker in civil status records] has existed in the country since 1998, not a single case of successful legal gender recognition has been reported to date’ (paragraph 74). Performance of gender-affirming health care is now punishable through a fine, a temporary occupational ban, or imprisonment for 1 to 4 years. Official crime statistics have, as of mid-2026, not registered any criminal cases for providing prohibited gender-affirming health care (see Trans rights and Arrest, detention, and prosecution of LGBT+ people).

4.1.8 Representatives of the ruling Georgian Dream party as well as pro-government media platforms frequently engage in homophobic and transphobic rhetoric, for instance during the 2024 pre-election period, during the adoption of recent rights-restricting legislation, and during periods of heightened visibility of the LGBT+ community such as Pride Month. Public officials also regularly portray LGBT+ activism as ‘propaganda’ as part of a wider anti-European and anti-liberal rhetoric that is tied in with the promotion of ‘traditional’ Georgian values which adds to the marginalisation of LGBT+ people (see Statements of public officials and state-aligned media).

4.1.9 In the sources consulted (see Bibliography), there were no documented cases in which a person or organisation was fined, convicted, or formally punished for actions prohibited by the 2024 Law on the Protection of Family Values and Minors. No official data on dispensed administrative penalties relating to ‘popularisation’ was available (see Arrest, detention, and prosecution of LGBT+ people and Violence against LGBT+ people).

4.1.10 There is limited information in sources consulted (see Bibliography) on police treatment. While one source reported instances of detention and prosecution of LGBT+ people who were themselves victims of assaults, the only example listed was a case that occurred in 2017 and resulted in an administrative fine. A further source made a general reference to instances of violence and harassment by state actors against LGBT+ people but provided no examples. During the 2024/ 2025 demonstrations against the Georgian Dream government, individuals whose appearance deviated from conventional gender presentations were reportedly particularly affected by police violence and exposed to homophobic hate speech by state authorities. However, security forces’ response during protests, and in the context of unrest at that time, is not necessarily representative of broader state treatment outside that specific environment (see Arrest, detention, and prosecution of LGBT+ people and Violence against LGBT+ people).

4.1.11 For further guidance on assessing risk, see the Asylum Instructions on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status, on Sexual identity issues in the asylum claim, and Gender identity issues in the asylum claim.

4.2 Risk from non-state actors

4.2.1 LGBT+ people in Georgia are, in general, unlikely to face a real risk of persecution or serious harm from non-state actors. The onus is on the person to demonstrate otherwise. LGBT+ people may experience discrimination, harassment, social exclusion, threats, and violence from non-state actors. Each case must be considered on its facts, taking account of the nature, severity and cumulative impact of any treatment experienced by the person.

4.2.2 Entrenched stereotypes and prejudice against people of diverse SOGIE continue to exist in Georgian society, with discriminatory attitudes being particularly pronounced among more rural populations. The Georgian Orthodox Church, to which 82% of the total population of Georgia belongs, frames LGBT+ issues as a threat to ‘traditional’ Georgian values and culture, fuelling stigma, discrimination, and harassment of persons of diverse SOGIE (see Demography, Lived experience, Public attitudes, and Treatment by the public and family members).

4.2.3 The Asylum Instruction on Sexual identity issues in the asylum claim notes that ‘[d]iscrimination and societal disapproval may not in themselves amount to persecution but, if expressed in an extreme way and without effective protection from the State, then outright hostility, general discriminatory measures and the cumulative effects of harassment, threats and restrictions can constitute persecution’ (page 16).

4.2.4 Conversion therapy is not banned however there is limited information on whether it occurs in practise. There is reference to ‘several cases’ of psychiatric intervention for children in 2024 but no further detail. There are no reported cases of surgery on intersex children or on non-consenting adults in sources consulted (see Conversion therapy and involuntary medical practices)

4.2.5 Spaces for the LGBT+ community to gather are limited and largely concentrated in Tbilisi. According to one source, they have at times come under threat, but no further detail on the nature or consequences of the threat was provided. Persons of diverse SOGIE are unable to enjoy the right to assembly and freedom of expression following the adoption of the Law of Georgia on the Protection of Family Values and Minors and recent changes to the Law on Assemblies and Demonstrations. In the sources consulted (see Bibliography), there were no records of recently organised demonstrations or Pride events in Georgia (see Lived experience, Visibility and activism, and Provisions relating to awareness-raising and activism).

4.2.6 While support organisations exist, they face challenges. Community outreach has become increasingly difficult, offices and staff homes have been vandalised and financial resources have decreased. New ‘foreign agent’ legislation has been introduced, granting the state the power to monitor activities, finances, internal communications, and documents of organisations that receive more than 20% of their funding from abroad. They also enable the state to restrict foreign funding and support to areas that align with the government’s interests, and make the grant of foreign funds dependent on state approval. Support organisations are thus increasingly unable to continue support and service provision programmes, particularly outside major cities (see Support organisations).

4.2.7 People of diverse SOGIE face systemic barriers to healthcare, employment, and education that render them vulnerable to physical and socio-economic hardship. This vulnerability is exacerbated where an individual’s diverse SOGIE intersects with other socio-economic or demographic vulnerabilities, such as belonging to an ethnic or religious minority, being an internally displaced person, or disability (see Access to services).

4.2.8 Stigma, a lack of specialised medical training, discriminatory attitudes and self-censorship of medical professionals, as well as financial barriers affect the LGBT+ community’s access to healthcare. This situation has worsened with the adoption of the Law on the Protection of Family Values and Minors, as its ban on gender-affirming healthcare creates significant challenges for trans and gender-diverse individuals undergoing treatment and for those with congenital conditions requiring continuous diagnostics and treatment. The non-governmental organisation (NGO) Equality Movement provides access to HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis treatment and self-testing kits. The effects of the Covid pandemic and the radicalisation of political and societal homophobia in Georgia have reportedly exacerbated the LGBT+ community’s mental health needs, while new legislation restricting foreign funding of CSOs has limited their ability to raise funds for support programmes. CSOs are therefore unable to fully cover the LGBT+ community’s unmet healthcare needs (see Access to healthcare).

4.2.9 Homophobic bullying and discrimination occurs in schools as well as higher and vocational education institutions, albeit slightly less in the latter two. The involvement of some school administrations and academic personnel is reported. While sexual education had never been fully integrated into Georgia’s school curricula, the Law on the Protection of Family Values and Minors now explicitly prohibits the dissemination of information on diverse SOGIE in educational settings and to minors (see Access to education).

4.2.10 Discrimination in the workplace based on sexual orientation and gender identity reportedly occurs during recruitment as well as employment and can serve as ground for termination. This compels many LGBT+ persons to conceal their SOGIE in the workplace. While many persons of diverse SOGIE are integrated in the labour market, employment is frequently precarious and poorly paid. Trans people face greater exclusion from the labour market, leading many to work in the informal economy and engage in sex work, often under abusive conditions and some when they are minors (see Access to employment).

4.2.11 Homophobic and transphobic hate speech and threats, including death threats, against people of diverse SOGIE on social media have increased in recent years. Several cases of blackmailing through the dissemination of personal information, including forced ‘coming out’ of individuals, have been reported. Far-right groups have repeatedly spread discriminatory and inciting rhetoric and mobilised disruptive public protests and counter-demonstrations against LGBT+ events such as IDAHOT, Tbilisi Pride, conferences, and cultural events, leading the organisation Tbilisi Pride to largely suspend its activities and close its office in 2025. However, in the sources consulted (see Bibliography), there were no reports of public LGBT+ events taking place in 2025 or 2026. Familial or friendly association with a person of diverse SOGIE may expose the family member or friend to threats and stigmatisation (see Hate speech and Treatment by the public and family members).

4.2.12 According to reports by civil society and the media, violent hate crimes against members of the LGBT+ community and support organisations have become more frequent in recent years, but are underreported in official statistics as victims frequently refrain from reporting crimes to the authorities. Violent hate crimes are perpetrated both in the public and the domestic spheres, and include physical assault, domestic abuse, and sexual harassment. Official Georgian statistics on hate crimes most often record the social relation between perpetrator and victim as stranger or acquaintance, with intimate partners, parents, and other family members recorded as perpetrators in a few instances only. However, since official Georgian hate crime statistics reportedly only capture a part of the overall anti-LGBT+ violence, this breakdown may be inaccurate (see Public attitudes, Protection, and Violent hate crimes).

4.2.13 According to a report by the Office of the Belgian Commissioner General for Refugees and Stateless Persons (OFPRA), most societal violence against LGBT+ people occurs within the family. The OFPRA report noted that experiences varied between LGBT+ people and that gay and bisexual men and trans women were more likely to experience a breakdown in family relations than lesbian women and trans men, indicating familial treatment is likely to depend on a range of factors (see Protection, Lived experience, and Treatment by the public and family members).

4.2.14 Individuals whose physical appearance does not conform to binary norms of femininity or masculinity may be more likely to experience violence and harassment in public, irrespective of their actual SOGIE. Two high profile cases of violence against trans people were reported in the media in 2025, one being a murder for which the perpetrator was convicted. There are also reports of a growing number of assaults against LGBT+ individuals during meetings scheduled through dating applications. Homophobic and transphobic violence has historically increased during periods of heightened LGBT+ visibility such as IDAHOT, Pride Month, and Tbilisi Pride in 2021 and 2023. However, since there are no documented cases of public LGBT+ events taking place since 2024, including due to Tbilisi Pride’s suspending its activities and closing of its office in 2025, it is difficult to ascertain to what extent this still occurs (see Violent hate crimes).

4.2.15 If a LGBT+ person is not ‘out’ about or conceals their sexual orientation and/or gender identity, consider why this is the case. If it is because the person fears persecution or serious harm and this is well-founded, they are likely to require asylum or humanitarian protection.

4.2.16 For further guidance on assessing risk, see the Asylum Instructions on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status, on Sexual identity issues in the asylum claim and Gender identity issues in the asylum claim.

5. Protection

5.1.1 A person who has a well-founded fear of persecution or serious harm from a non-state actor is unlikely to be able to obtain protection from the state. This is because, in general, it is able but not willing to offer effective protection.

5.1.2 State protection mechanisms for people of diverse SOGIE have in recent years been weakened through the dissolution of the Gender Equality Council as well as the removal of LGBT+ issues from the parliament’s Gender Equality Concept, the National Strategy for the Protection of Human Rights and the related Action Plan (see New state policy and legislation affecting LGBT+ people).

5.1.3 Official statistics on the investigation, prosecution, and conviction for SOGIE-related hate crimes show a decreasing trend over the past five years. While the number of initiated criminal investigations decreased from 106 in 2021 to 28 in 2025, the number of launched prosecutions decreased from 69 in 2021 to only 3 in 2025, with no hate crimes based on gender identity recorded anymore. Whereas the number of convictions has seen a less pronounced decline, this statistic can reasonably be expected to follow the trend of the launched prosecutions given the procedural link (see Protection).

5.1.4 While the declining trends in the official statistics could signify an actual decrease in SOGIE-related hate crimes, this conflicts with reports of civil society organisations and media that consistently point to increased violence and underreporting of crimes to law enforcement authorities. Violent responses to anti-government demonstrations and the use of offensive and homophobic language by law enforcement officers have eroded trust in the police and other state institutions. Victims of hate crimes thus rarely report incidents to the police as they fear discrimination, that they will not be believed, or inaction by law enforcement officers (see Protection).

5.1.5 The Georgian authorities have furthermore repeatedly failed to provide effective protection to LGBT+ persons against attacks, especially in the context of Pride events. Although violent groups had announced their intentions to disrupt the 2021 and 2023 Tbilisi Pride events in advance, the police failed to take effective measures to prevent them. The police did, however, evacuate participants of the 2023 Tbilisi Pride. While some anti-LGBT+ protesters were arrested and prosecuted for theft, damage, and destruction of property during the 2021 and 2023 Tbilisi Pride events, the instigators and organisers of the attacks have not been brought to justice. In subsequent years, Tbilisi Pride has refrained from organising further Pride events citing safety concerns (see Protection and Response to violence during the 2021 and 2023 Pride events).

5.1.6 Lawyers’ organisations report that the Law on Family Values and Protection of Minors has affected legal assistance available to LGBT+ individuals, as lawyers feel discouraged from providing legal support out of a fear it could be interpreted as facilitating prohibited action. Judicial and administrative bodies are reported to systematically delay the provision of information and the scheduling of proceedings (see Protection).

5.1.7 Access to human rights protection mechanisms have declined as submissions by LGBT+ people are routinely rejected or ignored. In addition, the removal of ‘gender identity’ as a protected ground from legislation in 2025 has left victims of police discrimination based on gender identity with no legal basis for a challenge. Crimes motivated by gender or gender identity are no longer an aggravating circumstance under the Criminal Code. While the relevant provisions under the Criminal Code were only rarely enforced in the past, a trans or gender-diverse victim now no longer has a legal basis for redress and protection. While the Public Defender’s Office had previously served as an outspoken supporter of the LGBT+ community in anti-discrimination efforts, since the election of a new Public Defender in 2023 it is perceived to be substantially aligned with government interests (see Protection and The Public Defender (Ombudsman)).

5.1.8 For further guidance on assessing state protection, see the Asylum Instructions on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status, on Sexual identity issues in the asylum claim, and Gender identity issues in the asylum claim.

6. Internal relocation

6.1.1 In general, a person with a well-founded fear of persecution or serious harm from a non-state or rogue state actor is likely to be able to internally relocate to escape that risk. This includes, but is not limited to, the capital city of Tbilisi. Each case must be considered on its facts.

6.1.2 Georgia is a small country with a population of approximately 3.9 million. Approximately 1.3 million people live in the capital of Tbilisi, and safe social spaces for LGBT+ are reportedly available. Further, urban areas such as the capital are reported to provide more socio-economic opportunities than rural areas. Discriminatory societal attitudes remain, however, relatively consistent throughout the country.

6.1.3 Internal relocation will not be an option if it depends on the person concealing their sexual orientation and/or gender identity in the proposed new location if the reason (or one of the reasons) is a fear of persecution. Each case must be considered on its facts.

6.1.4 For further guidance on internal relocation and factors to consider, see the Asylum Instructions on Assessing Credibility and Refugee Status, Sexual identity issues in the asylum claim, and Gender identity issues in the asylum claim.

7. Certification

7.1.1 Where a claim is refused, it is unlikely to be certifiable as ‘clearly unfounded’ under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002.

7.1.2 Each case must be considered on its individual facts.

7.1.3 For further guidance on certification, see Certification of Protection and Human Rights claims under section 94 of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 (clearly unfounded claims).

8. Demography

8.1.1 According to the results of the 2024 Population Census of Georgia, the population of Georgia stood at 3.9 million as of November 2024. Approximately 1.3 million Georgians live in the country’s capital Tbilisi[footnote 1].

8.1.2 The 2024 census results furthermore indicate that approximately 3.2 million Georgians adhere to the Georgian Orthodox faith, or 82% of the total population[footnote 2].

8.1.3 The French Office for the Protection of Refugees and Stateless Persons (OFPRA) noted in a report on the situation of sexual minorities in Georgia (OFPRA 2025 Report), published in French in March 2025: ‘The Georgian LGBT+ community was estimated to number several thousand people in 2019. In 2018, the NGO Tanadgoma estimated the population of gay men at approximately 18,500. The majority of the LGBT+ community lives in Tbilisi, Batumi and Kutaisi.’[footnote 3]

The first sentence of the quoted paragraph paraphrases a report by the UN’s Independent Expert on protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity on his visit to Georgia that was published in May 2019 and noted: ‘… at a rough estimate, the trans community in Batumi could be as high as 100 persons and […] thousands of gay men or men who had sex with men, as well as lesbian and bisexual persons, were active members of social networks.’[footnote 4]

9. Legal framework

9.1 Anti-discrimination provisions

9.1.1 Article 11 of the Constitution of Georgia, adopted in 1995 and most recently amended in 2018, stipulates that all persons are equal before the law and prohibits any discrimination. The article contains a non-exhaustive list of potential discrimination grounds that does not explicitly refer to sexual orientation, gender identity and expression (SOGIE)[footnote 5].

9.1.2 The Law of Georgia on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination, adopted in 2014 in Georgian language and amended most recently in 2025, is intended to eliminate every form of discrimination and ensure equal rights of every person under the legislation of Georgia, irrespective of, inter alia, gender and sexual orientation[footnote 6]. Whereas the 2014 version of the law specifically referred to “gender identity and expression” as well[footnote 7], a 2025 amendment deleted this reference[footnote 8].

For information on LGBT+ individuals’ access to services such as healthcare, education, and employment, see Access to services.

9.1.3 Article 2.3 of the Labour Code of Georgia, adopted in 2010 in Georgian language and amended most recently in 2025, prohibits any discrimination in labour and pre-contractual relations, including, inter alia, on the grounds of gender and sexual orientation[footnote 9].

For information on accessibility of the labour market for LGBT+ individuals, see Access to employment.

9.1.4 Article 53 1 of the Criminal Code of Georgia, adopted in 1999 in Georgian language and amended most recently in 2026, provides that the commission of a crime on the basis of sexual orientation constitutes an aggravating circumstance for all crimes under the Code[footnote 10]. Whereas previous versions of the Criminal Code also listed “gender” and “gender identity” as aggravating reasons for intolerance[footnote 11], a 2025 amendment deleted these references[footnote 12].

9.2 Provisions relating to same-sex relationships, marriage, and civil union

9.2.1 Article 30 of the Constitution of Georgia, defines marriage as a union of a woman and a man for the purpose of founding a family[footnote 13]. This definition was introduced by the 2017 law On Amendments to the Constitution of Georgia[footnote 14].

9.2.2 Similarly, article 4 of the Law of Georgia on the Protection of Family Values and Minors, adopted in 2024, defines marriage in Georgia as a voluntary union exclusively between a man and a woman for the purpose of forming a family. It explicitly prohibits the registration or legal recognition of same-sex unions as marriage, including those concluded abroad which have no legal validity in Georgia[footnote 15].

9.2.3 Article 5 of the same law prohibits the adoption of a child by a non-heterosexual person[footnote 16]. The prohibition is replicated in article 4 of the Law of Georgia on Adoption and Foster Care[footnote 17].

9.2.4 The undated International Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex Association (ILGA) World Database entry for Georgia indicated that ‘[t]he Criminal Code (2000) of Georgia removed the pre-existing sodomy provisions that were carried through from the Soviet Union period’[footnote 18], thus decriminalising consensual same-sex sexual acts.

9.3 Trans rights

9.3.1 Article 5 of the Law of Georgia on the Protection of Family Values and Minors prohibits the adoption of a child by a person that does not identify with a biological sex or that identifies with a sex different from their biological sex[footnote 19].

9.3.2 Article 6 of the same law prohibits procedures intended to assign or reassign an individual to a different sex through medical means[footnote 20].

9.3.3 Article 176 1 of the Criminal Code of Georgia defines the punishment for the performance of a surgical operation or other medical treatment intended to assign an individual to a different sex as a fine, an occupational ban of up to three years, or imprisonment for one to four years[footnote 21]. See Arrest, detention, and prosecution of LGBT+ people.

9.3.4 Article 7 of the Law of Georgia on the Protection of Family Values and Minors prohibits registering or later changing a person’s sex in civil status records to anything other than their biological sex. It also prohibits indicating a different sex in identity documents or other official state-issued documents as well as recognising or enforcing foreign court decisions that assign a person a non-biological or non-binary sex[footnote 22].

9.4 Provisions relating to awareness-raising and activism

9.4.1 Article 3 of the Law of Georgia on the Protection of Family Values and Minors defines the term ‘popularisation’ as the positive or exemplary portrayal of same-sex relationships as well as of identification with a sex different from one’s biological sex or with a non-binary sex[footnote 23].

9.4.2 Article 8 of the same law prohibits ‘popularisation’ as defined in article 3 in educational institutions[footnote 24].

9.4.3 Article 172 10 of the Administrative Offences Code of Georgia, adopted in 1984 and last amended in June 2026, sets the punishment for ‘popularisation’ in educational institutions as a fine of ₾1,500 Georgian lari (GEL) [approximately £425 GBP[footnote 25]] for a natural person [individual human beings] and ₾4,000 GEL [approximately £1,133 GBP[footnote 26]] for a legal person [private or public organisations][footnote 27].

9.4.4 Article 9 of the Law of Georgia on the Protection of Family Values and Minors prohibits ‘popularisation’ as defined in article 3 by broadcasters and in advertisements, as well as through direct communication with a minor[footnote 28].

9.4.5 Article 172 10 of the Administrative Offences Code of Georgia sets the punishment for ‘popularisation’ in advertisements as a fine of ₾800 GEL [approximately £226 GBP[footnote 29]] for a natural person and ₾2,500 GEL [approximately £708 GBP[footnote 30]] for a legal person. ‘Popularisation’ towards a minor is punishable by a fine of ₾1,000 GEL [approximately £283 GBP[footnote 31]] for a natural person and ₾3,000 GEL [approximately £850 GBP[footnote 32]] for a legal person[footnote 33].

9.4.6 Article 10 of the Law of Georgia on the Protection of Family Values and Minors prohibits public assemblies and manifestations aimed at ‘popularisation’ as defined in article 3[footnote 34].

9.4.7 Article 9(6) of the Law of Georgia on Assemblies and Demonstrations, adopted in 1997 and last amended in 2025, prohibits demonstrations aimed at ‘popularisation’ as defined in article 3 of the Law of Georgia on the Protection of Family Values and Minors. Article 13(8) of the Law of Georgia on Assemblies and Demonstrations stipulates that, where a demonstration is held in contravention of this prohibition, law enforcement authorities may terminate it if the event hasn’t ceased 15 minutes after participants have been informed of its unlawful nature. Article 14(1) of the same law sets out that the Ministry of Internal Affairs is authorised to prohibit the holding of such events[footnote 35].

See also New state policy and legislation affecting LGBT+ people.

10. LGBT+ community

10.1 Lived experience

10.1.1 Following a visit to Georgia, the UN’s Independent Expert on protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity published a report in May 2019, the most recent available. It noted that ‘… systemic factors deny lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans and gender diverse persons the right to live free and equal in Georgia.’[footnote 36]

10.1.2 The same report continued:

‘[The Independent Expert] encountered the pervasive notion that the aspects inherent to the sexual orientation or gender identity of lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans and gender diverse persons living in Georgia were sinful, shameful or pathologic. The societal goal appears to perpetuate a vision of Georgia as a country composed exclusively of heterosexual, cisgender persons. As a result, the majority view is that lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans and gender diverse persons must conceal their identity if they want to be recognized as citizens respectful of mores and values qualified as “good”. Those convictions are fuelled and reinforced by agents of the church, tolerated and at times sponsored by politicians, governmental and law enforcement agents, and replicated by mass and social media.’[footnote 37]

10.1.3 The same report also noted: ‘The consequences of this concerted attack are real. They include the threat for members of the community of exposure to violence and exclusion from health, housing, work and economic opportunities, and indeed all other basic elements fundamental to a person’s quest for happiness, through mechanisms of social exclusion and ostracism.’[footnote 38]

10.1.4 The same report further stated:

‘Each lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans or gender diverse person in Georgia puts in place some sort of survival strategy. Very few are protected by status or wealth; others leave the country and break their family bonds to seek asylum elsewhere. Those who remain face the choice of revealing their true self and being subjected to certain violence and discrimination or concealing that essential aspect of their identity and living in a parallel world. For them, the fate is the invisibility of their needs and their realities, non-existence in official data and constant fear of exposure.’[footnote 39]

10.1.5 In the 2022 Gallup World Poll, 9% of survey respondents in Georgia indicated that their city or area was a good place to live for gay or lesbian people[footnote 40]. In Georgia, the poll consisted of 1,000 face-to-face interviews conducted between August and October 2022, with South Ossetia and Abkhazia as well as small and remote mountainous villages excluded[footnote 41].

10.1.6 David Rypel, a London-based ‘social scientist specialising in ethnographic research’[footnote 42] noted in a statement provided to research network Asylos in August 2024:

‘… [S]everal of my LGBTQI [research] participants felt that they had to shield their parents from societal discrimination. Especially those whose families live in smaller villages and communities said they were reluctant to come out or be ‘visible’ in their hometowns to protect their families from peer pressure and shaming. In some cases, this was their parents’ request, and at least one of my participants was discouraged by their mother from reporting their victimisation to the police out of fear that she might become the target of her neighbours’ abuse. Therefore, LGBTQI people must sometimes assume the role of shielding their families from societal discrimination at their own expense.’[footnote 43]

10.1.7 The OFPRA 2025 Report furthermore observed:

‘The decriminalisation of homosexuality in 2000 encouraged the development of […] meeting places. The arrival of the internet enabled LGBT+ people to communicate online through the websites gay.ge and lesbi.ge, as well as through private groups on social media and Russian-language forums. Since the 2010s, certain bars and nightlife venues […] have provided spaces for freedom and socialisation for members of the LGBT+ community. However, these venues have at times come under threat.’[footnote 44] The source did not expand further on the nature of the threat.

10.1.8 The OFPRA 2025 Report also stated: ‘As safe social spaces for LGBT+ people are limited and largely concentrated in Tbilisi, online platforms provide members of the community with opportunities to socialise. However, they also make them more vulnerable to cyberharassment.’[footnote 45]

10.1.9 Equality Movement, a Georgian NGO providing social, legal, and healthcare services for women and the LGBTQ community[footnote 46], noted in a statement to the CGRS in September 2025, published in the CGRS 2025 Report: ‘… [T]he safe spaces for community gatherings have become extremely limited. Practically, nowadays only queer friendly clubs, bars and community organization’s offices … [are] left as a space for community’s secure socialization.’[footnote 47]

10.1.10 Equality Movement further observed in a statement to the CGRS that was made in July 2025 and published in the CGRS 2025 Report:

‘The family members of LGBTQ+ individuals are also affected. The spread of anti-LGBT propaganda, combined with the recent legal developments has intensified already widespread homo-, bi-, and transphobic hatred in society. This has led to an increase in incidents of bullying, threats, and discrimination, particularly on social media and in public spaces. Given the extreme polarization within society, these issues are becoming even more severe.’[footnote 48]

10.1.11 The same statement continued: ‘[It n]eeds to be stressed that not only families of LGBTQ+ individuals, but also those of professionals working in LGBTQ+ community organizations, are at risk of deteriorating mental health, along with increasing social and economic marginalization. In some cases, the risk may also extend to physical danger.’[footnote 49]

10.1.12 Equality Movement also observed in a statement to the CGRS that:

‘The social and economic challenges faced by the LGBTI community are relatively harsher in the peripheral spaces of the country. The problems, on the one hand, are caused by the uneven distribution of socio-economic resources, which creates a development gap between urban and rural spaces. As a result, structural poverty is more acute in small towns and villages, further exacerbating the socio-economic vulnerability of LGBTI individuals living in these areas.’[footnote 50]

10.2 Returnees

10.2.1 Equality Movement noted in a statement published in the CGRS 2025 Report ‘It is rare to find LGBTQ+ individuals returning to Georgia. The very few who are compelled to return—due to reasons such as denial of asylum in other countries, family obligations, or other personal emergencies—face extreme social and economic exclusion, along with significant risks to their physical safety. … Most LGBTQ+ individuals who have recently returned are actively seeking ways to leave the country again.’[footnote 51]

10.2.2 Equality Movement further observed in a statement to the CGRS that was made in September 2025 and also published in the CGRS 2025 Report in the same month:

‘… [T]he lives of those LGBTQ+ individuals returning are just as full of challenges as those of community members who never left the country. They face serious difficulties related to a radicalized security context as well as social and economic exclusion, such as limited access to employment, healthcare, and other essential issues.

‘The difference may not be large, but it is important to emphasize: when LGBTQ+ individuals are forced to leave Georgia, they must quit their jobs, give up housing, and sometimes lose social connections as well. The difficulties they faced before remain the same or can even worsen when they are compelled to return. … [T]he most common challenges for returnees are ongoing experiences of bullying and discrimination, sometimes including verbal and physical assault, as well as difficulties in finding stable employment to cover housing and basic necessities.’[footnote 52]

10.3 Visibility and activism

10.3.1 The US Department of State’s 2023 Country Report on Human Rights Practices, published in April 2024 and covering events of 2023 (USSD 2023 Report), noted: ‘The ability of LGBTQI+ individuals to assemble in public or private or to form associations – as well as the ability of LGBTQI+ organizations to legally register or convene events – was limited.’[footnote 53]

10.3.2 The US Department of State’s 2024 Country Report on Human Rights Practices in Georgia (USSD 2024 Report) did not contain a section on acts of violence, criminalization, and other abuses based on sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics[footnote 54].

10.3.3 The OFPRA 2025 Report observed:

‘The issue of visibility divides the community between those who favour discretion in order to continue carrying out grassroots work, and those who favour greater visibility in order to change public attitudes.

‘On the one hand, organisations such as Equality Movement, Women’s Initiatives Supporting Group, Temida, and Tanadgoma support a more discreet approach so that they can continue their field work safely, particularly with sex workers, people who use injectable drugs, and people living with HIV. Several LGBT+ artists’ collectives have adopted the same strategy, seeking to advance their cause through cultural means without drawing excessive attention to themselves and thereby avoiding direct confrontation.

‘On the other hand, organisations such as Tbilisi Pride—which is responsible for organising events during Pride Month—and GrlzWave pursue extensive social media communication strategies that reach a broad audience. Although activists consider this level of visibility necessary for strengthening connections within the community and raising awareness of issues affecting LGBT+ people, it requires them to implement additional security measures, such as Tbilisi Pride’s practice of verifying the identities of participants before events.

‘Most activists working to defend the rights of LGBT+ persons and, more broadly, human rights, know one another and come together to speak with a unified voice whenever their rights are under attack, despite differing views on the form that their activism should take.’[footnote 55]

10.3.4 The same report noted: ‘Various events are organised discreetly by the LGBT+ community in Tbilisi, without significant publicity. For example, it is possible to attend screenings of certain Georgian LGBT+-themed films…

‘More public events are organised by LGBT+ persons to mark the International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia on 17 May, and during the months of June and July, when Tbilisi Pride holds its Pride Festival. However, this period is generally also the time when violence is at its highest. For this reason, in 2024, LGBT+ rights organisations chose to cancel public events. Accordingly, the NGO Tbilisi Pride decided not to organise a Pride Festival in 2024, citing a context in which hatred towards the LGBT+ community was being instrumentalised in the run-up to the parliamentary elections of 26 October that year.’[footnote 56]

10.3.5 Human Rights Watch reported in its World Report 2025, covering events of 2024: ‘In 2024, the organizers of Tbilisi Pride refrained from holding in-person events during Pride Month, citing concerns over potential violence and hate rhetoric, compounded by introduction of the anti-LGBT legislation.’[footnote 57]

10.3.6 The Public Defender (Ombudsman) of Georgia published his 2024 Special Report ‘On the Situation of Equality and Combating and Preventing Discrimination’ (2024 Ombudsman Report) in May 2025, which stated:

‘The LGBTQ+ community in Georgia did not enjoy the constitutional right to assembly and demonstration in 2024. In the context of the right to assembly and demonstration, Article 10 of the Law of Georgia on the Protection of Family Values and Minors is noteworthy, which, among other things, prohibits assemblies aimed at promoting relationships between members of the same biological sex, expressed on the basis of sexual orientation. Although according to the legislative regulation, only the kind of information and actions that present specific issues positively and/or as exemplary are considered popularization, the exact scope of the prohibition remains unclear, which has a deterrent effect in terms of exercising freedom of expression.’[footnote 58]

10.3.7 Equality Movement observed in a statement to the CGRS, published in the CGRS 2025 Report in September 2025 that ‘… the relatively visible part of the community or individuals who openly position as LGBTI activists are more likely to be targeted for physical danger or discrimination.’[footnote 59]

10.3.8 The same statement continued:

‘… [H]uman rights activists focused to raise the visibility of the community are increasingly targeted for demonization and marginalization. They are often labeled by propagandistic media outlets as a “threat to children” or “enemies of the church.” It should be stressed that associating prominent human rights activists with the LGBTI community - regardless of their actual identity - has become a common tactic to undermine their work and discredit their public image. Due to physical threats fueled by such endeavors of the ruling party, many human rights activists had been forced to flee the country.’[footnote 60]

10.3.9 Equality Movement also noted in a statement to CGRS, made in July 2025 and published in the CGRS 2025 Report in September 2025:

‘Since the law [on Family Values and the Protection of Minors] came into force, LGBTQ+ content … has practically disappeared from the media landscape. Nowadays, concerns about the challenges faced by the community are raised only by a limited number of online media outlets and LGBTQ+ community organizations.

‘… [M]edia coverage of LGBTQ+ issues is significantly limited. The focus is primarily on broadcasting anti-gender legal developments and, occasionally, on a few critical incidents involving activists who are relatively well-known to the public. Notably, positive coverage of LGBTQ+ issues has completely disappeared.’[footnote 61]

10.3.10 The ILGA noted in its latest Annual Review of the Human Rights Situation of Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex People in Europe and Central Asia (2026 ILGA Report), published in 2026 and covering January to December 2025:

‘The Pride movement in Georgia, led by Tbilisi Pride, has constituted one of the most visible tests of equality, civic space, and democratic governance in the country. Pride initiatives have represented not only advocacy for LGBTI rights but also a broader indicator of Georgia’s commitment to human rights standards and the protection of freedom of assembly. Pride-related events, including the March for Dignity in 2021 and the Pride Festival in 2023, were violently disrupted by far-right groups.’ [footnote 62] See also Response to violence during the 2021 and 2023 Pride events.

10.3.11 Patrycja Grzebyk, rapporteur of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE), noted in her ‘Report on Developments in Georgia in Respect of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms since Spring 2024’ (OSCE 2026 Report), published in March 2026:

‘… [The Law on Family Values and the Protection of Minors] constitutes a restriction of … [freedom of expression and freedom of assembly] as it directly prohibits almost any public expression on certain topics and bans assemblies related to a certain theme.

‘… [T]he key category of ‘popularization’ is defined in markedly broad and vague terms as essentially any information or actions aimed at presenting issues related to gender identity, sexual orientation or incest in positive or exemplary light. This could be interpreted as prohibiting education or awareness-raising campaigns aimed at promoting sexual health or even as requiring LGBT+ individuals to conceal their sexual orientation or gender identity in their daily lives. Furthermore, … essentially equating same-sex relationships and gender identity other than conforming to prevailing social norms with incest is stigmatizing and degrading and has no place in countries that claim to uphold human dignity and human rights.’[footnote 63]

10.3.12 In the OSCE 2026 Report, the rapporteur furthermore noted with regards to the Law on Family Values and the Protection of Minors:

‘… [R]estrictions put in place by the said law are so severe that they may be held as infringing upon the very essence of [freedom of expression and freedom of assembly] … In wholly banning public gatherings organized around the theme of LGBT+ rights the law in question essentially nullifies the right to assembly. In banning any expression that would ‘popularize’ LGBT+ rights it can be interpreted as wholly denying the right to speak on those issues or even expressing sexual or gender identities of the persons concerned.’[footnote 64]

10.4.1 Equality Movement is a Georgian NGO which provides social, legal, and healthcare services for women and the LGBTQ community. At the time of writing, its webpage remained accessible online, with content updated in recent weeks[footnote 65] (see Healthcare).

10.4.2 The Women’s Initiative Supporting Group (WISG) is a feminist organisation advocating for women’s rights, particularly those of lesbian and bisexual women and transe people. Its webpage remained accessible online at the time of writing, with content uploaded in recent weeks[footnote 66].

10.4.3 Tbilisi Pride is an organisation focused on strengthening the LGBT+ community and conducting advocacy aimed at influencing the political agenda and public opinion in Georgia. Its webpage remained accessible online at the time of writing, with content uploaded in recent weeks[footnote 67]. In recent months, the organisation’s social media channels have only advertised events for the Georgian LGBT+ community abroad to where its staff appear to have relocated[footnote 68].

10.4.4 The online publication ’Queer’ publishes articles and information on issues affecting the LGBTQ+ community of Georgia. Its webpage remained accessible at the time of writing[footnote 69].

10.4.5 Queer Initiative is an activist collective advocating for LGBTQ+ rights and equality in Georgia. At the time of writing, its social media channels remained active[footnote 70].

10.4.6 The Caucasus Research Resource Center, a ‘network of research, resource and training centers established in 2003 in the capital cities of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Georgia’[footnote 71], noted in a report on civil society organisations working on gender equality in Georgia, published in 2024: ‘The difficulties of working with state agencies are particularly hard for organizations working on LGBTQI+ issues. Due to their infrequent involvement in discussions and working processes, they struggle to participate in the decision-making process, and their recommendations often go unconsidered.’[footnote 72]

10.4.7 The ILGA noted in its 2025 Annual Review of the Human Rights Situation of Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Trans and Intersex People in Europe and Central Asia (2025 ILGA Report), published in 2025 and covering the year 2024: ‘In the spring of 2024, Tbilisi Pride office was vandalised twice by unidentified persons likely having ties with the [ruling party] Georgian Dream.’[footnote 73]

10.4.8 The OFPRA 2025 Report observed: ‘Several NGOs and initiatives advocating for the rights of LGBT+ persons exist in Georgia. Emigration and exposure to violence result in a high turnover rate among these organisations and their members.’ [footnote 74]

10.4.9 The same report noted that ‘… several human rights organisations include LGBT+ rights within their programmes. These include the Social Justice Center (SJC), GrlzWave, Sapari, the Human Rights House, the Human Rights Center, the International Society for Fair Elections and Democracy (ISFED), the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association (GYLA), Transparency International Georgia, and the Open Society Georgia Foundation (OSGF).’[footnote 75]

10.4.10 The WISG noted in a report on the eradication of LGBTQI+ issues from state policy in Georgia (WISG 2025 Report), published in May 2025:

‘LGBTQI+ organizations in Georgia have recently faced significant challenges regarding safety and security. A homophobic environment has persisted for many years, but the situation worsened during the summer of 2024 when the attacks on the offices of LGBTQI+ organizations and acts of vandalism became increasingly frequent. Between May and June, buildings belonging to non-governmental organizations, as well as the homes of activists, were targeted—splashed with red paint, with eggs and posted with insulting messages directed at LGBTQI+ activists and organizational representatives.’[footnote 76]

10.4.11 Equality Movement reported in a statement to the CGRS that was made in July 2025 and published in the CGRS 2025 Report in September 2025:

‘… [T]he financial stability of LGBTQ+ organizations had … been undermined by the sudden closure of the U.S.-funded programs, which alarmingly limited the financial resources available to them. All local community NGOs - which serve as the only source of support for vulnerable groups - now face serious financial challenges that limit their ability to sustain program and service provision. Many are no longer able to cover staff salaries, putting the continuity of essential services at immediate risk …’[footnote 77]

10.4.12 Equality Movement observed in a statement to the CGRS that was published in the CGRS 2025 Report in September 2025:

‘… [D]ue to the shortage of financial resources LGBTI community organizations face difficulties operating nationwide, and those based in regional areas are relatively weak financially, which limits access to support programs and services for people living outside major cities. In addition, the internal “research on the updated needs of the LGBTQ+ community in relation to healthcare, psychosocial and legal services” conducted by Equality Movement revealed that regional community organizations face the absence of LGBTI-sensitive service provider staff. Furthermore, the regional activists outline that in recent periods, community outreach became unsafe and the majority of them are identifying themselves labeled and targeted.’[footnote 78]

10.4.13 The 2026 ILGA Report reported: ‘In recent years, Georgia has undergone a marked authoritarian shift, characterised by increasing restrictions on civil society and non-governmental organisations, alongside intensified anti-LGBTI rhetoric. In this context, Tbilisi Pride reported that it was compelled in 2025 to largely suspend its activities, close its office, and relocate staff, citing the inability to organise Pride Week safely under prevailing conditions.’[footnote 79] See also Visibility and activism.

10.4.14 Human Rights Watch noted in an article published in July 2026: ‘The authorities have […] used homophobic rhetoric to delegitimize independent organizations by portraying them as promoters of “LGBT propaganda” and opponents of traditional values.’[footnote 80] See also Statements of public officials and state-aligned media.

10.4.15 Human Rights Watch reported in the same article ‘The government […] denied approval for a grant supporting an LGBT rights organization’s healthcare and harm reduction project for marginalized communities. The group’s director told Human Rights Watch that the authorities provided no explanation for the rejection.’[footnote 81]

10.4.16 Human Rights Watch noted in the same article:

‘Organizations reported increasing self-censorship and fear of criminal prosecution against their leaders and staff. Groups working on LGBT rights described the pressure as especially acute.

‘The Grlz Wave [a queer-feminist organisation based in Tbilisi[footnote 82]] director said, “We had to shift to a regime of self-censorship,” particularly on queer issues. “It is now extremely difficult to find respondents willing to appear in videos on LGBT topics. Even openly out individuals refuse visibility.”

‘Organizations have also curtailed broader programmatic work. The director of a group providing social and healthcare services to vulnerable communities said that “self-censorship was one of the most severe effects.” The organization suspended all cooperation with the government and halted its advocacy work, including a planned 2025 public awareness campaign on sex education, because of the risk that authorities could invoke the “LGBT propaganda” law or the foreign agents law.’[footnote 83]

11. State treatment

11.1 New state policy and legislation affecting LGBT+ people

11.1.1 Equality Movement noted in a report on LGBTQ+ Rights Violations in Georgia in 2024, published in March 2025:

‘The homophobic intentions supported by the ruling party have been gradually transformed into institutional decisions. In 2022/2023, the terminology referring to gender identity or sexual orientation completely disappeared from the strategic documents of national importance. First of all, the LGBTQ+ community has been fully removed from Parliament’s Gender Equality Concept document. It must be emphasized that the document now defines the concept of gender equality exclusively between ‘women’ and ‘men’. A similar scenario occurred during the development of the National Strategy for the Protection of Human Rights of Georgia for 2022-2030 and the respective Action Plan for 2024-2026. Despite the critics and joint efforts of local civil society organizations (CSOs) and international organizations, none of the LGBTQ+ issues have been integrated into the documents.’[footnote 84]

11.1.2 The Coalition for Equality, a NGO-consortium that ‘aims to strengthen the mandate of anti-discrimination mechanisms and promote effective efforts in combating discrimination’[footnote 85], stated in a report on the state of right of equality in Georgia, released in March 2025:

‘With the exclusion of LGBTQI+ issues from State policy documents and the introduction of discriminatory legislation, the challenges faced by the community have escalated into a practice of state-orchestrated violence. The impact of the anti-LGBTQI+ Law extends across multiple fields and aspects of life for community members. On the one hand, the Law [on the Protection of Family Values and Minors] contradicts the principle of equality enshrined in the Constitution of Georgia, and, on the other hand, it violates international standards and obligations that the country has committed to uphold. Beyond the risks of censorship, healthcare, employment, and education, the Law imposes restrictions on fundamental rights, threatening freedom of expression and assembly while exposing the entire community to discrimination.’[footnote 86]

The source did not expand on what it meant by ‘practice of state-orchestrated violence’ and did not provide examples of this in practice.

11.1.3 The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), noted in a report submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in April 2025:

‘On 17 September 2024, the Georgian Parliament adopted a law “on family values and protection of minors” and a related package of amendments. The law imposes restrictions on education, public discussion and gatherings that may be discriminatory based on sexual orientation and gender identity. It reinforces negative stereotypes by equating same-sex relationships with incest, denies legal recognition to same-sex couples and transgender people, restricts access to healthcare and undermines efforts to fight HIV/AIDS…

‘According to publicly available information, the legislative amendments include administrative and criminal sanctions effectively banning certain forms of LGBTQI+ activism, related scientific and professional activities and transgender-specific healthcare services.’[footnote 87]

11.1.4 Human Rights Watch reported in its World Report 2025, covering events of 2024:

‘In September, parliament adopted anti-LGBT amendments imposing discriminatory restrictions on rights to education, health, freedom of expression, and peaceful assembly. The amendments ban gender-affirming medical care for trans people, same-sex marriage, and adoption by same-sex couples. They also prohibit positive references to LGBT people in literature, film, and media, as well as in schools and at public gatherings.

‘In June, the Venice Commission [the Council of Europe’s advisory body on constitutional matters] urged the authorities not to adopt the amendments, warning that their mere introduction could deepen the already hostile and stigmatizing atmosphere against LGBT individuals in Georgia.’[footnote 88]

11.1.5 The USSD 2024 Report, published in August 2025, noted: ‘Notable negative human rights developments in Georgia during the year included the entry into force of the … so-called law On Family Values and Protection of Minors that criminalized certain types of expression …’[footnote 89]

11.1.6 The Office of the Belgian Commissioner General for Refugees and Stateless Persons (CGRS) noted in a report (CGRS 2025 Report), published in Dutch in September 2025:

‘On 3 April 2024, the ruling party Georgian Dream announced the Foreign Agents Law, officially titled the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Following a presidential veto on 18 May 2024, Parliament nevertheless approved the law ten days later, and it entered into force on 3 June 2024. Under the law, organisations and media companies that receive more than 20% of their funding from abroad are given two months to register as organisations “pursuing the interests of a foreign power”. … [I]n a small and relatively poor country such as Georgia, this applies to virtually all NGOs… The Ministry of Justice has the authority to monitor the activities, finances, internal communications and documents of registered organisations.’[footnote 90]

11.1.7 The same report noted:

‘In early April 2025, Parliament adopted a national version of the US Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA)… Under the new FARA, a foreign agent is defined as any person (legal or natural) who is under the control of, or acts at the direction of, a foreign power and acts in the interests of that foreign power. … [T]his means that, unlike the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence, FARA will also apply to individuals. Failure to comply with the law may be punishable by up to five years’ imprisonment, a fine of up to 10,000 GEL (approximately €3,202), or both.’[footnote 91]

11.1.8 The 2026 ILGA Report noted:

‘In April, the Georgian Dream party advanced a series of legislative amendments in the first reading, including significant changes to the Law on Gender Equality. These amendments removed the term “gender” from the text, replacing all references to “gender identity” or “gender equality” with the narrower formulation “equality between women and men.” Accordingly, the 2014 Law of Georgia on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination was also amended with “gender identity” being removed from the list of protected grounds, and the Gender Equality Committee [the correct name is Gender Equality Council[footnote 92]] was formally dissolved. The Georgian Dream party justified the initiation of these amendments by claiming that the term “gender” had been purposely introduced into Georgian legislation under foreign influence as a “reflection of the global processes”.’[footnote 93]

11.1.9 The OSCE 2026 Report noted:

‘In September 2024, the parliament adopted the Law on Family Values and the Protection of Minors… The law essentially equates, for its purposes, same-sex relationships and transgender identity with incest. In so doing, it prohibits the ‘popularization’ of all, including in broadcasting, education and during public gatherings. The law also bans gender-affirming care, including through surgical intervention, indication in civil acts and identity documents of a sex different than the one assigned at birth, same-sex marriage and legal recognition of same-sex relationships other than marriage, and adoption by LGBT+ couples or individuals.’[footnote 94]

11.1.10 In the same report, the OSCE rapporteur stated that ‘… the enactment of the Law on Family Values, paired with homophobic and transphobic rhetoric of Georgian politicians and the widespread stigmatization of LGBT+ individuals in the public sphere, certainly contributes to the overall atmosphere, ripe for … deplorable displays of hatred.’[footnote 95]

11.1.11 The OHCHR observed in a report submitted to the UN Human Rights Council in April 2026:

‘In 2025, legislative amendments were enacted to more than 15 laws, with changes including replacing the terms “gender” and “gender equality” with “women and men” and “equality between women and men”, respectively. Amendments to the Law on Assemblies and Demonstrations included discriminatory restrictions based on sexual orientation and gender identity, and gender identity was removed from the list of prohibited grounds in various laws concerning discrimination, aggravating circumstances for hate crimes, and provisions related to incitement to hatred and violence.’[footnote 96]

11.1.12 Human Rights Watch reported in an article published in July 2026:

‘Amendments [to the Law on Grants] adopted in April 2025 required foreign donors to obtain government approval before awarding grants, and penalized organizations that accept a foreign grant without authorization with fines equivalent to double the amount received. A subsequent government decree made approval conditional on foreign grants aligning with “the government’s program, key strategic documents, and the state’s interests.” Further amendments adopted in June 2025 expanded the definition of a “grant” to include various forms of technical and expert assistance…’[footnote 97] See also Support organisations.

In the sources consulted (see Bibliography), no publicly reported cases in which an individual or organisation had actually been fined, detained, arrested, prosecuted, or convicted specifically for breaching the provisions of the new Law of Georgia on the Protection of Family Values and Minors were identified. See also Arrest, detention, and prosecution of LGBT+ people.

11.2 Statements of public officials and state-aligned media

11.2.1 The Democracy Research Institute, a Tbilisi-based ‘public policy think tank’[footnote 98], noted in a report on anti-gender rhetoric and gender stereotypes in social media, published in 2024:

‘In Georgia, the main actors of the anti-gender discourse are representatives of the “Georgian Dream,” its satellite political forces, openly pro-government media platforms, and far-right groups. Their main focus is on women’s and children’s rights, religious values, the institution of the family, the rights of sexual minorities, and issues of gender identity and sexuality. The more or less fragmented anti-gender campaigns of far-right groups were transformed by the government into a powerful political instrument, and over time, it became the lead sponsor of the homophobic, sexist, and anti-gender campaign.’[footnote 99]

11.2.2 The same report noted:

11.3 Arrest, detention, and prosecution of LGBT+ people

11.3.1 The OFPRA 2025 Report noted in March 2025: ‘In some cases, … [police forces] have detained and prosecuted LGBT+ persons who were themselves victims of assaults, as occurred in 2017 in the case of Levan Berianidze and Tornike Kusiani.’[footnote 114]

The LGBT+ activists Levan Berianidze and Tornike Kusiani were arrested by the Georgian police and charged with hooliganism and civil disobedience in August 2017, after having been attacked by several men[footnote 115]. Both individuals were released on the day of their arrest and found guilty of the alleged offences by the Batumi City Court one day later, each receiving a fine of ₾300 GEL [approximately £85 GBP[footnote 116]][footnote 117].

11.3.2 The investigative agencies of Georgia regularly release unified reports on registered crime statistics. The 2025 end-of-year report and the 2026 mid-year report both list 0 cases registered under article 176 1 of the Criminal Code of Georgia which relates to violations of the prohibition of gender-affirming health care established by the Law of Georgia “On the Protection of Family Values and Minors”[footnote 118],[footnote 119]. See also Trans rights.

11.3.3 While the Georgian Ministry of Internal Affairs publishes statistical tables on selected administrative offences[footnote 120], it does not provide data on administrative offences relating to the Law of Georgia “On the Protection of Family Values and Minors”, specifically Article 172 10 of the Administrative Offences Code of Georgia that relates to ‘popularisation’. See also Provisions relating to awareness-raising and activism.

11.3.4 In the sources consulted (see Bibliography), no further reports on arrests, detention, or prosecution of LGBT+ people were available. See also New state policy and legislation affecting LGBT+ people.
