12. Societal treatment

12.1 Public attitudes

12.1.1 The Integrated Values Surveys combined responses from the cross-sectional longitudinal European Values Study and the World Values Survey[footnote 177], who jointly conducted a survey of 2,194 adults residing in Georgia between 2017 and 2022, comprising a national-wide random representative sample[footnote 178]. The survey responses indicated that 93.1% of the sampled Georgian population expressed the opinion that homosexuality can never or rarely be justified[footnote 179]. No further disaggregation of survey data was available.

12.1.2 UN Women’s Gender Equality Attitudes Study in Georgia was conducted from January to February 2024 through face-to-face interviews with 1,238 individuals aged 16 or above, measuring the prevalence of discriminatory attitudes and gender-based stereotypes. Two thirds of the study participants were women, and one third men. 41% of interviews were conducted in Tbilisi, 31% in other urban areas, and 28% in rural settlements. The study report noted: ‘Only 11 per cent of the Georgian public believes that it is difficult for most men to run for elected office in the country … However, twice as many people (22 per cent) believe that it is difficult for most women to do the same… A majority (57 per cent) believes that it is difficult for LGBTQI+ individuals who do not hide their orientation.’[footnote 180]

12.1.3 The same study included the below graphic, indicating in percentages the surveyed population’s responses to the question ‘In general, how easy is it for sexual minority women (lesbian, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex) who do not hide their sexual orientation / sexual minority men (gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex) who do not hide their sexual orientation to run for elected office in Georgia?’ The 11-point scale was recoded into three categories: Scores of 0–3 were categorized as “difficult”, scores of 4–6 were categorized as “neutral”, and scores of 7–10 were categorized as “easy”[footnote 181].

12.1.4 The Council of Europe’s Commissioner for Human Rights observed in a statement, published in March 2024, that ‘… entrenched harmful stereotypes and prejudice against LGBTI people […] still prevail in segments of Georgian society …’[footnote 182]

12.1.5 The Caucasus Research Resource Centers conduct the Caucasus Barometer Georgia, a regular household survey about social-economic issues and political attitudes. The most recent edition of the Caucasus Barometer Georgia was conducted between April and May 2024 among 1,509 adults, excluding populations living in territories affected by military conflict, in particular South Ossetia and Abkhazia[footnote 183]. 73% of respondents did not approve of doing business with a sexual minority person, while 19% approved[footnote 184].

12.1.6 In the same survey, 9% of respondents answered ‘sexual minorities’ in response to the question ‘Which of these people would you not wish to have [as] your neighbors most?’, the third most common response after ‘drug addicts’ (36%) and ‘criminals’ (32%)[footnote 185].

12.1.7 The OFPRA 2025 Report stated: ‘In 2021, 84% of Georgians considered sexual relations between two people of the same sex to be inherently wrong. While some sources report a slight decline in homophobic and transphobic attitudes in Georgian society, other surveys indicate that the proportion of Georgians who consider homosexuality unacceptable has not decreased.’[footnote 186]

12.1.8 The same report noted:

‘According to a study published in 2022 by the organisation [Women’s Initiative Supporting Group] … with the support of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), “the share of the population that believes protecting the rights of the LGBT+ community is important increased from 21% to 27%” between 2016 and 2021. The study also found an increase in the proportion of Georgians who regard restrictions on LGBT+ rights as unacceptable and who believe that the State does not respond adequately to the violence and discrimination experienced by LGBT+ persons.

‘However, the study emphasised that these changes were mainly linked to the attitudes of women, as well as younger people and residents of the capital, because “male respondents have hardly changed their views on this issue”, a pattern also seen among older people and rural populations. In addition, homosexuality is more accepted among women than among men.

‘Despite this relative change in attitudes, LGBT+ persons remain among the most marginalised and least protected groups in Georgia.’[footnote 187]

12.2 Treatment by the public and family members

12.2.1 The Public Defender (Ombudsman) of Georgia noted in his 2023 report on the situation of protection of human rights and freedoms in Georgia, published in May 2024:

‘As in previous years, the rights situation of LGBT+ people remains an important/serious challenge. Members of the LGBT+ community still face violence, discrimination, and harassment, and this is caused by homophobic attitudes, hate crimes, and other discriminatory attitudes in society. Individuals with far-right ideologies, through their actions and statements, contribute to the spread of homophobic sentiments, incite discrimination and, at the same time, commit actions that are often manifested in serious violations of the rights of LGBT+ people.’[footnote 188]

12.2.2 Social scientist David Rypel noted in a statement to the research organisation Asylos in August 2024: ‘Several of my [research] participants or their friends and acquaintances were thrown out of their homes by their parents upon their coming out, potentially to prevent bringing ‘shame’ to the household.’[footnote 189]

12.2.3 The WISG 2025 Report observed:

‘The Church remains one of the most trusted institutions in Georgia, and its stance on moral issues—particularly regarding sexual orientation and gender identity—significantly shapes public opinion. This environment fuels ultra-right movements, which, in collaboration with religious authorities, frame LGBTQI+ issues as a threat to Georgian identity, culture, and national values. Despite numerous violent acts carried out by these groups, the effective enforcement of justice has consistently been inadequate, fostering the perception that these groups operate with the backing of the government.’[footnote 190]

12.2.4 The OFPRA 2025 Report noted:

‘Since the 2000s, the Patriarchate of the Georgian Orthodox Church has opposed the visibility of LGBT+ people, whom it regards as “destabilising the country and public life” by “promoting a non-traditional way of life”. In 2014, the Georgian Orthodox Church established Family Purity Day on 17 May—the same date as the International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia (IDAHOBIT)—and in July 2023 it called for legislation prohibiting LGBT+ propaganda.’[footnote 191]

12.2.5 The OFPRA 2025 Report also stated, summarising several older reports that were published between 2019 and 2022:

‘The family is the primary social sphere in which violence against LGBT+ people occurs, often leading to individuals leaving the family home after coming out, encountering difficulties in finding alternative accommodation, and experiencing a degree of economic insecurity. Nearly one in five LGBT+ individuals report being isolated from their family and friends. Associating with LGBT+ people may also expose their relatives and close associates to threats and stigmatisation. However, family attitudes vary depending on sexual orientation and gender expression: gay and bisexual men, as well as transgender women, are more likely to experience a breakdown in family relations than lesbian women and transgender men.’[footnote 192]

The ‘nearly one in five’ figure on social isolation quoted above stems from a 2020 report by the Georgian CSO Human Rights Education and Monitoring Centre, which summarised 320 survey responses that were gathered via face-to-face interviews with LGBT+ people in Georgia between September and December 2019. Over 86% of the study participants were aged between 18 and 29 years, and approximately two thirds were living in the capital Tbilisi. Due to this sampling method, the study’s findings cannot be generalised to the whole LGBT+ population of Georgia. The study found that 19% of respondents reported to have experienced social isolation from friends and family in the last two years[footnote 193]. Notably, the results stem from the pre-Covid period.

12.2.6 The Bertelsmann Stiftung, ‘a private operating foundation which engages in evidence-based and solely nonprofit activities’[footnote 194] noted in its Transformation Index 2026: ‘… [S]exual minorities face heightened stigma and discrimination, particularly following the enforcement of the 2024 law “On the Protection of Family Values and Minors,” which is widely seen as homophobic and transphobic.’[footnote 195]

12.3 Hate speech

12.3.1 Equality Movement stated in its report on LGBTQ+ rights violations in Georgia, published in March 2025, that ‘the number of cases processed by [Equality Movement] concerning homophobic hate speech or gender-based discrimination on social networks, particularly TikTok, was remarkably high in 2024…

‘Also, during the reporting period, several cases were processed involving the disclosure of information about the private lives of LGBTQ+ individuals, with or without the use of social networks, and cases of blackmailing through the dissemination of personal information, including forced “coming out” of individuals.’[footnote 196]

12.3.2 The WISG 2025 Report noted: ‘… [The] main focus [of Georgian ultra-right groups] lies in promoting nationalist and homophobic rhetoric, which they actively spread through social media and their own media platforms. These platforms are often used to disseminate anti-Western propaganda and incite hatred within society. A vivid example is Alt-Info, which for years has been vocal in spreading pro-Russian and homophobic narratives. Although Alt-Info ceased broadcasting in 2024, other members of the organization have continued using all available media channels to spread hate and reinforce anti-Western sentiment.’[footnote 197]

12.3.3 The same report stated that ‘… in Georgia, ultra-right groups that promote anti-gender narratives also tend to propagate homophobic discourse. These groups frequently accuse various media outlets and non-governmental organizations of engaging in the so-called “promoting of corruption” and “corrupting the nation.”’[footnote 198]

12.3.4 The same report continued:

‘Ultra-right groups are most active during events organized by LGBTQI+ groups or organizations. Their primary methods of mobilization include public protests and counter demonstrations, especially during events such as IDAHOT, Tbilisi Pride, various conferences, and cultural festivals. These groups often resort to physical attacks, threats of violence, organized aggression, and hate speech—none of which are effectively addressed by the state.’[footnote 199]

12.3.5 Equality Movement noted in a statement to CGRS, made in July 2025 and published in the CGRS 2025 Report in September 2025, that ‘… the use of homophobic hate speech and threats, including death threats, has alarmingly increased on social media platforms. In addition, it has become normalized for individuals, especially for those who actively participate in anti-Russian protests to be bullied simply by being labeled as members of, or associated with, the LGBTQ+ community that increases their risks of physical vulnerability.’[footnote 200]

12.3.6 Equality Movement stated in its 2025 annual report, published in May 2026 and covering 2025, that its legal team had provided legal assistance in 136 cases, including 96 cases newly opened during the year. 30 cases related to violence and threats[footnote 201].

12.4 Violent hate crimes

12.4.1 Social scientist David Rypel observed in a statement to the research organisation Asylos in August 2024: ‘The general impression among the participants of my qualitative research was that gay cis men and trans women have a higher chance of being assaulted on the street, making them more visible victims of anti-queer violence.’[footnote 202]

12.4.2 The same expert noted: ‘Lesbian cis women face less visible forms of oppression, such as domestic abuse, or gender-based sexual harassment, such as slut-shaming, and violence that might not always be recognised as ‘anti-queer.’’[footnote 203]

12.4.3 Radio Free Europe/ Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), a news outlet that seeks ‘to promote democratic values by providing accurate, uncensored news and open debate in countries where a free press is threatened and disinformation is pervasive’[footnote 204], reported in an article published in October 2024: ‘Nata Talikishvili, a transgender activist in Georgia, was attacked in Tbilisi on October 20, just a month after the killing of another transgender woman, Kesaria Abramidze, reflecting the worsening climate for LGBT rights in the South Caucasus country. The Interior Ministry told RFE/RL a suspect was arrested for allegedly insulting Talikishvili and hitting her with a brick, leaving her with a concussion.’[footnote 205]

12.4.4 In the sources consulted (see Bibliography), no information was available about the outcome of the criminal prosecution for the attack against Nata Talikishvili.

12.4.5 InterpressNews, a Tbilisi-based Georgian news agency[footnote 206], stated in an article published in July 2025, that ‘… [t]he Tbilisi Court of Appeals has upheld, without changes, the guilty verdict against Beka Jaiani for the deliberate murder of Kesaria Abramidze committed with particular cruelty on the grounds of gender. This information was released by the Prosecutor’s Office of Georgia.’[footnote 207]

12.4.6 The i Paper noted in an article published in October 2024: ‘LGBT people in Georgia are facing increasing violence and persecution after the government passed a law that imposed sweeping restrictions on the community. Many LGBTQ+ people have described living in fear, with some forced to flee the Caucasus country because of threats and discrimination about their sexualities and gender.’[footnote 208]

12.4.7 The same article observed: ‘Ilga-Europe, an LGBTI advocacy group, says there has been a sharp rise in violence against the community, including vandalism of organisations Tbilisi Pride and WISG, and violent threats – including death threats against LGBT activists and their families.

‘“People in my community have experienced physical violence, homelessness, extreme poverty, and mental health challenges,” … says [Tamar Jakeli, director of Tbilisi Pride], noting how these effects are rooted in the way LGTBQ+ people are treated in Georgia by the government, employers, and friends and family. “Police are usually very unhelpful and even hostile…”’[footnote 209]

12.4.8 The 2025 ILGA Report noted:

‘Just one day after the Parliament of Georgia passed the anti LGBTI law, a celebrity trans woman, Kesaria Abramidze was found brutally murdered in her apartment. The subsequent investigation pertains to premeditated murder with aggravating circumstances of special cruelty based on gender identity. In October, a month after Kesaria’s murder, renowned trans activist Nata Talikishvili was physically attacked with a brick, resulting in a concussion.’[footnote 210]

12.4.9 Equality Movement stated in its report on LGBTQ+ rights violations in Georgia, published in March 2025:

‘… [S]everal attacks on LGBTQ+ community members followed an identical pattern in 2024. The incidents happened during meetings scheduled through dating applications. For instance, [Equality Movement] … was contacted by a citizen of a foreign country stating that after he arrived at such a date, unidentified people appeared at the scene, who physically assaulted and verbally abused him. … [T]he person refrained from reporting the incident to the police. … [V]ictims of other dating app-related attacks have not contacted law enforcement agencies either.’[footnote 211]

12.4.10 The OFPRA 2025 Report noted that ‘[hate crimes against LGBT+ persons in Georgia] … are rarely reported to the authorities, in whom LGBT+ people have little confidence. Moreover, discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity is rarely treated as an aggravating circumstance.’[footnote 212]

12.4.11 The OFPRA 2025 Report further observed:

‘Each year, from May to July, around Pride month, NGOs observe an increase in homophobic and transphobic violence and assaults. Violence against LGBT+ persons reaches its peak during the period when they are most visible, stretching from the International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia and Transphobia (17 May) until July, when Tbilisi Pride holds its Pride festival. Spikes in violence may also occur when information is disseminated by ultra-conservative groups, as happened during the screening of Levan Akin’s film And Then We Danced.’[footnote 213]

12.4.12 The OFPRA 2025 Report also stated: ‘Within the LGBT+ community, transgender persons are the most exposed to violence.’[footnote 214]

12.4.13 The WISG 2025 Report noted: ‘Transgender individuals are facing particular challenges. There have been documented cases of verbal abuse in public, as well as physical assaults—two of which escalated into physical attacks.’[footnote 215]

12.4.14 Equality Movement noted in a statement to CGRS, made in July 2025 and published in the CGRS 2025 Report in September 2025: ‘… [T]he state no longer classifies hate crimes on SOGI grounds separately. In addition, given that the majority of incidents go unreported, the official statistics fail to reflect reality.’[footnote 216]

12.4.15 Equality Movement also observed in its statement to the CGRS:

‘Equality Movement’s lawyers report that, alongside the massive anti-LGBT campaign and related legal developments, there has been a noticeable increase in attacks motivated by transphobia. Some transgender individuals and other LGBTQ+ community members who remain in Georgia are facing severe physical security risks - being verbally and physically assaulted multiple times per month - which ultimately forces many to flee the country.’[footnote 217]

12.4.16 Equality Movement further stated: ‘Particularly concerning are emerging trends in SOGI based violence, such as attacks on LGBTQ+ individuals orchestrated by luring them through dating applications.’[footnote 218]

12.4.17 Equality Movement noted in a second statement to the CGRS, made in September 2025 and equally published in the CGRS 2025 Report in the same month:

‘The risks to physical safety for lesbian, gay, bisexual, and non-binary persons are closely tied to their appearance. Individuals whose physical presentation does not conform to binary norms of femininity or masculinity often become immediate targets of violence and harassment. Moreover, victims of homophobic aggression are not always members of the community. In some cases, individuals are targeted simply because their appearance deviates from culturally accepted norms. Hatred in society is increasing alongside the intensification of homophobic rhetoric.’[footnote 219]

12.4.18 The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe’s (OSCE) Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights compiles an annual hate crime report on participating OSCE states, with a focus on specific bias motivations[footnote 220]. The 2024 Hate Crime Report, published in November 2025, records 27 anti-LGBTI hate crimes for Georgia[footnote 221].

12.4.19 The 2026 ILGA Report observed:

‘In 2025, the continued prevalence and systemic nature of hate crimes motivated by sexual orientation or gender identity remains one of the most pressing challenges faced by the LGBTI community in Georgia. Nonetheless, a mismatch between the official statistics and reality was induced by the obstacles hindering the effective prevention and investigation of SOGI-based hate crimes — such as delays in launching investigations, granting victims the status of ‘aggrieved party’, or properly qualifying criminal cases, combined with the lack of sensitivity and awareness among police officers, prosecutors, and investigators.’[footnote 222]

12.4.20 The same report noted:

‘Data collected by civil society organisations in 2025 indicate that, despite a decrease in officially recorded cases in recent years, bias-motivated crimes based on sexual orientation and gender identity remain a significant concern.’[footnote 223]

For information on the arrest and prosecution of crimes committed against LGBT+ people, see Protection.

12.5 Conversion therapy and involuntary medical practices

12.5.1 The undated ILGA World Database entry for Georgia indicates that ‘… laws in force in Georgia do not regulate or restrict sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression change efforts (SOGIECE), regularly known as “conversion therapies”.’[footnote 224]

12.5.2 The USSD 2023 Report observed: ‘So-called conversion therapy practices were not banned. According to Tbilisi Pride, there were several cases of parents taking children to a psychiatrist in an attempt to change the sexual orientation or gender identity or expression of the child.’[footnote 225]

12.5.3 The same report continued: ‘There were no reports of surgeries performed on intersex children or nonconsenting intersex adults. The law and medical associations did not limit these practices or speak out against them.’[footnote 226]

13. Access to services

13.1 General

13.1.1 Equality Movement noted in its report on LGBTQ+ rights violations in Georgia, published in March 2025:

‘The number of state services responding to the needs of vulnerable groups is critically limited in Georgia. For many years now, the non-governmental sector has tried to bridge this gap. In this regard, the LGBTQ+ community faces particular exclusion. Over the years, due to the inadequate implementation of anti-discriminatory mechanisms and domination of oppressive discourses in society, especially among professional groups, the state services designed to mitigate and overcome the challenges faced by the community remain absent.[footnote 227]

13.1.2 Equality Movement further noted in a statement to the CGRS, made in September 2025 and published in the CGRS 2025 Report in the same month:

‘… [S]ince 2022 no comprehensive research has been carried out on socio-economic vulnerability of the community. However, Equality Movement’s systematic observations, conducted to design and adjust programs and services in line with the community’s needs, reveal that systemic barriers to education, employment, healthcare, and other areas remain persistent. Equality Movement’s internal “research on the updated needs of the LGBTQ+ community in relation to healthcare, psychosocial and legal services” conducted in the beginning of 2025 shows that some of these barriers have further intensified.’[footnote 228]

13.1.3 Equality Movement also observed in a statement to the CGRS that was published in the CGRS 2025 Report in September 2025:

‘Multiple factors can be fueling the physical and socio-economic vulnerability of certain LGBTI individuals. Due to failures of state policy and institutions, factors such as belonging to an ethnic or religious minority, being a migrant or internally displaced person, or living with a disability all contribute to structural poverty. When these socio-economic or demographic vulnerabilities intersect with SOGIESC-related issues, the barriers to fully realizing human rights and achieving wellbeing become even more severe.’[footnote 229]

13.1.4 The same statement continued:

‘An individual’s socio-economic vulnerability is often shaped by their family’s socio-economic conditions. The situation becomes even more severe when LGBTI individuals experience domestic violence. At this stage, the cycle of socio-economic exclusion frequently begins: neglected by their families or forced to leave home at an early age to escape violence, many are deprived of access to proper education, which in turn limits their employment opportunities to low-wage jobs or sex work, which contributes to additional social challenges and physical security risks.’[footnote 230]

13.2 Access to healthcare

13.2.1 UNAIDS, the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV and AIDS, issued a press release in October 2024 that expressed ‘deep concern over the recently adopted anti-LGBTQ+ legislation in Georgia, which poses serious risks to public health and human rights…

‘These discriminatory laws violate fundamental rights to autonomy, dignity, and equality, exacerbating stigma and hindering LGBTQ+ people’s access to essential health services. This undermines Georgia’s efforts to end AIDS and combat other infectious diseases.’[footnote 231]

13.2.2 The OFPRA 2025 Report observed: ‘LGBT+ people are more exposed to mental health problems due to their vulnerability and persistent discrimination. When needed, some turn to community organisations for support. According to Coalition for Equality, a coalition of five human rights NGOs, members of the LGBT+ community do not seek state-funded psychiatric support services because they do not trust them.’[footnote 232]

13.2.3 The same report noted: ‘Among transgender people, the main barrier to healthcare is the lack of training among medical staff regarding their specific needs.

‘The COVID-19 pandemic particularly affected the mental health of the LGBT+ community, as restrictions on movement increased the isolation of LGBT+ individuals from their community.

‘Stigma towards people living with HIV/AIDS persists in Georgia and creates additional barriers to accessing testing. The NGO Equality Movement provides access to HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) treatment as well as self-testing kits that can be delivered to people’s homes and are advertised through the dating application Grindr. Although HIV testing and treatment are free of charge in Georgia, medical care and treatment for other illnesses that may be contracted as a result of HIV/AIDS remain very expensive.’[footnote 233]

13.2.4 The 2024 Ombudsman Report further noted:

‘It is important to emphasize the impact of the law [of Georgia on the Protection of Family Values and Minors] on the right to life and health. According to Article 6 of the law, it is prohibited to perform a surgical operation or to use any other medical manipulation in order to assign a person to a gender different from his/her biological sex. This restriction is not limited to surgical operations and applies to all types of medical interventions, which poses serious challenges for people undergoing gender-affirming surgery, since access to medical services is critically important for their life and health, which will be at risk if medical personnel refuse to provide necessary medical services on the grounds of non-compliance with the law. The right to health implies access to necessary medical care without discrimination.’[footnote 234]

13.2.5 The three non-governmental organisations ECOM – Eurasian Coalition on Health, Rights, Gender and Sexual Diversity, Equality Movement, and Tbilisi Pride in July 2025 issued a joint submission to the 51st Universal Periodic Review session in January 2026. In this document, the organisations noted:

‘In the absence of comprehensive state protection, civil society organizations including LGBT led and allied NGOs have assumed a critical role in the realization of the right to health … These organizations have been central in the delivery of HIV prevention and care services, provision of psychosocial support, legal aid, human rights monitoring, and policy advocacy. Their work has been instrumental in partially filling gaps in the national healthcare system, particularly in addressing the needs of men who have sex with men (MSM), transgender persons, and other key populations. However, due to budget constraints and the lack of respective medical licenses, they are unable to fully meet the demand for physical and mental health services coming from the community.’[footnote 235]

13.2.6 Equality Movement indicated in its 2025 annual report, published in May 2026, that 12,665 beneficiaries had received a basic package of essential tools for preventing the spread of HIV and sexually transmitted infections in 2025. Furthermore, 8,247 beneficiaries had received voluntary counselling and testing services for HIV and other sexually transmitted infections, including viral hepatitis (B and C) and syphilis. 484 beneficiaries were enrolled in the HIV Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) programme[footnote 236].

13.2.7 The WISG 2025 Report observed:

‘The latest legislative amendments have had a severely negative impact on healthcare services for the LGBTQI+ community. Under the newly adopted law, transgender individuals are entirely deprived of access to healthcare. The law imposes criminal liability on doctors or other healthcare professionals who provide medical services to LGBTQI+ individuals, banning healthcare procedures that are vital for their health and survival or other manipulations.’[footnote 237]

13.2.8 The same report continued: ‘Access to healthcare has never been fully available to the LGBTQI+ community in Georgia. State policy has failed to improve the situation over the years, and the absence of national guidelines and protocols has long been a problem. Even discriminatory attitudes within the healthcare system were widespread. Community members often felt compelled to hide their sexual orientation or gender identity—or avoid healthcare services altogether—due to fears of stigma, harassment, or degrading treatment.

‘… [T]ransgender individuals have faced mistrust from medical personnel, inadequate service provision, and openly hostile attitudes.’[footnote 238]

13.2.9 Equality Movement noted in a statement to the CGRS, made in July 2025 and published in the CGRS 2025 Report in September 2025: ‘Self-censorship among medical professionals was already in effect even before the law was enacted - transgender individuals were denied access to essential healthcare services. Having no possibility to continue hormonal therapy or exercise right to health in a safe medical environment, forced numerous trans individuals to flee the country…

‘The service provider professionals report that the increasingly radicalized environment in the country, combined with constant stress and fear, has led to a severe deterioration of the community’s mental health. The demand for Equality Movement’s psycho-social care services has alarmingly raised in recent periods …’[footnote 239]

13.2.10 The same statement continued: ‘The adoption of the anti-LGBT law has had a profoundly negative impact on service and program provision. The criminalization of trans-specific healthcare has forced local LGBTQ+ organizations to shut down all gender affirming programs and services.’[footnote 240]

13.2.11 Equality Movement noted in a further statement to the CGRS, made in September 2025 and also published in the CGRS 2025 Report in the same month:

‘… LGBTI individuals’ access to healthcare is hindered by both financial and cultural factors. Economic exclusion deprives community members of sufficient resources not only for costly medical treatments but also for routine health needs, including medical check-ups and essential medications. The situation becomes even more severe for those with congenital conditions requiring continuous diagnostics and treatment. In many cases, community members are forced to take bank loans to meet urgent medical needs, which further exacerbates their vulnerability. As a result, crowdfunding has become a common means of financing treatment. However, supporters’ financial resources are themselves limited.’[footnote 241]

13.2.12 The same statement continued: ‘In addition to financial barriers, violations of medical ethics and mistreatment of patients motivated by homophobia are widespread in Georgia’s healthcare sector. Examples revealed by Equality Movement’s internal research conducted in the beginning of 2025 include the stigmatization of sexually transmitted diseases, the provision of ‘unofficial’ treatments by doctors, and suggestions to withhold medical diagnoses.’[footnote 242]

13.2.13 The same statement also observed:

‘Due to the severity of the problem, Equality Movement supports LGBTI individuals through ensuring their access to HIV and STDs-related prevention and treatment, advocating for PrEP and PEP, providing outreach in order to make medical services accessible for hidden community groups, providing certain medical consultations on the basis of organization’s resource centre or referring community members to “friendly” doctors, and in some cases even co-financing the certain medical bills. However, similar to Georgia’s broader civil society sector, the adoption of restrictive laws on NGOs and amendments to the Law on Grants have severely hindered international donors’ fundraising efforts. As a result, the financial resources of LGBTI community organizations are being depleted, creating a serious risk that even the limited access to medical care currently available will soon disappear.’[footnote 243]

13.2.14 The same statement noted:

‘Another pressing challenge is the limited access to mental health services. Due to state neglect, mental health is largely excluded from national healthcare policy. Consequently, access to such services remains financially unavailable, even for individuals with private insurance coverage. In recent years, the radicalization of political and institutional homophobia, significantly hindering the wellbeing and safety of LGBTI individuals, triggered various mental health-related issues. Through the course of 2024, approximately 60% of beneficiaries addressing the Equality Movement’s social worker service were redirected to the mental health services. Although the Equality Movement tries to increase the organizational capacity to fully meet the community’s mental health-related needs, it is always challenging to overcome the waiting lines for the psycho-social services. In case the grant giving won’t be reactivated in Georgia, by the beginning of 2026 the organization will be severely hindered in its ability to continue providing services.’[footnote 244]

13.2.15 The 2026 ILGA Report noted that ‘LGBTI persons remained particularly affected by stigma, confidentiality concerns, and discriminatory practices in healthcare, with trans people facing additional hurdles due to the absence of national protocols for trans-specific care, limited medical competences, and a lack of insurance coverage.’[footnote 245]

13.3 Access to education

13.3.1 The WISG 2025 Report noted: ‘LGBTQI+ individuals in Georgia continue to face various forms of harassment and discrimination within educational institutions. While universities and vocational schools tend to offer a slightly more open environment, homophobic attitudes from some students and professors remain a significant concern.’[footnote 246]

13.3.2 Equality Movement noted in a statement to the CGRS, made in September 2025 and published in the CGRS 2025 Report in the same month: ‘The barriers obstructing LGBTI individual’s access to education can be divided into two major parts: financial and cultural. While physical access to school education is largely ensured in Georgia, systemic poverty and the absence of family support often prevent LGBT individuals from continuing their studies beyond secondary school, leaving them without the financial means to pursue higher or vocational education.

‘In addition to financial obstacles, widespread bullying and discrimination in educational institutions - rooted in cultural barriers - significantly hinder the community’s access to education. Locally conducted studies confirm that homophobic bullying and discrimination remain pervasive across schools, as well as higher and vocational education institutions. These problems are driven by the absence of adequate anti-discrimination policies and mechanisms, while staff in educational institutions frequently lack the necessary qualifications to address cases of discrimination. Alarmingly, observations often indicate the involvement of school administration and academic personnel in bullying and discriminatory practices. Based on observations, it can be emphasized that in ‘exceptional’ cases where the educational process is not affected by homophobic oppression, it is achieved at the cost of concealing one’s identity.’[footnote 247]

13.3.3 The same statement continued: ‘It needs to be stressed that sexual education has never been properly incorporated into Georgia’s educational agenda. On the contrary, it has often been used as a tool to promote ‘cultural protectionism’. The lack of basic awareness of SOGIESC-related issues has further reinforced these barriers, significantly hindering the LGBTI community’s ability to properly exercise their right to education.’[footnote 248]

13.3.4 Equality Movement further observed in its statement to the CGRS:

‘The situation has drastically deteriorated after the adoption of the “Law on Family Values and Minors” that introduced additional barriers to educational inclusiveness and obstructed efforts to combat widespread homophobic discourses in society… In direct contradiction to the principle of inclusiveness, the law prohibits the incorporation of SOGIESC related information into all types of formal educational programs, as well as the dissemination and/or facilitating the dissemination of such information within formal educational institutions, including schools, universities, and vocational education centers. By imposing such uncompromising control over educational content, the law effectively enables state censorship and erects significant barriers to academic freedom. Furthermore, by banning direct communication with minors on matters of sexual orientation and gender identity the law eliminates the possibility of educating adolescents about fundamental concepts of gender and sexuality even in informal settings. According to the Equality Movement’s information, although the law has not yet been enforced, consequently, no educational institutions have been fined for violating it, students have already faced rejection of academic theses on SOGIESC-related topics by their supervisors or institutional administration.’[footnote 249]

13.3.5 The International LGBTQI Youth & Student Organisation (IGLYO), ‘the world’s largest network dedicated to LGBTQI young people and their rights’[footnote 250], noted in its LGBTQI Inclusive Education Report 2025:

‘Although the Law on General Education and the Law on Higher Education formally prohibit discrimination, there are no specific policies or programmes to foster tolerance toward diverse sexual orientations and gender identities. Likewise, there are no regulatory mechanisms in place to address bullying based on SOGIESC grounds.’[footnote 251]

13.3.6 The same report noted:

‘There is currently no mandatory teacher training on LGBTQI awareness for school teachers. NGOs have typically encountered obstacles in their efforts to promote awareness-raising initiatives among teachers…

‘The LGBTQI community organisation’s attempts to collaborate with relevant state institutions to train school teachers on gender and sexuality issues have largely been rejected. The situation has been further exacerbated by the adoption of the anti-LGBTQI law, which prohibits such discussions within formal educational institutions.’[footnote 252]

13.3.7 The same report stated: ‘Despite widespread LGBTQIphobia [sic] in educational institutions in Georgia, the government has failed to establish effective mechanisms to prevent and mitigate such incidents.’[footnote 253]

13.4 Access to employment

13.4.1 The USSD 2023 Report observed: ‘LGBTQI+ activists said discrimination in the workplace based on gender identity and sexual orientation remained widespread and underreported.’[footnote 254]

13.4.2 UN Women’s Gender Equality Attitudes Study in Georgia, implemented from January to February 2024 to measure the prevalence of discriminatory attitudes and gender-based stereotypes, noted: ‘The public is mostly in agreement that being hired as skilled workers is difficult for … LGBTQI+ individuals (lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer and intersex) who are public about their sexual orientation (61 per cent).’[footnote 255]

13.4.3 The same study included the below graphic, indicating in percentages the surveyed participants’ responses to the question ‘In general, how easy is it for most sexual minority women (lesbian, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex) who do not hide their sexual orientation / sexual minority men (gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex) who do not hide their sexual orientation to be hired as skilled workers in Georgia?’ The employed 11-point scale was recoded into three categories: Scores of 0–3 were categorized as “difficult”, scores of 4–6 were categorized as “neutral”, and scores of 7–10 were categorized as “easy”[footnote 256].

13.4.4 The OFPRA 2025 Report noted:

‘Most LGBT+ persons are integrated into the labour market, primarily in the service and cultural sectors, but more than half partially or completely conceal their gender identity and/or sexual orientation at work. As is often the case in Georgia, employment is frequently precarious and poorly paid, leading many individuals to hold multiple jobs: in 2020, 68% of LGBT+ persons were employed, and among them one in five held at least two jobs. These data derive from a study conducted before the COVID-19 pandemic, during which more than two out of three LGBT+ persons lost their jobs. Nearly one LGBT+ person in three reported experiencing discrimination in the workplace, and the majority did not seek assistance, either because they considered it unnecessary or believed that nothing could be done.’[footnote 257]

13.4.5 The OFPRA 2025 Report further observed:

‘Transgender persons, particularly transgender women, face greater exclusion from the labour market, notably because of the personal identification documents they are required to present. They are also the group most exposed to prostitution, often entering sex work after experiencing violence in previous employment. A quarter were minors when they began engaging in prostitution, and nearly 90% reported having experienced violence at the hands of a client.’[footnote 258]

13.4.6 The WISG 2025 Report stated: ‘Discrimination in the labour market is … widespread. … LGBTQI+ community members—particularly transgender individuals— face systemic inequality in employment. The lack of legal gender recognition mechanisms further exacerbates their exclusion, often forcing them into unofficial or exploitative working conditions.’[footnote 259]

13.4.7 The same report continued: ‘… LGBTQI+ individuals in Georgia struggle to find jobs with dignified conditions. Many are relegated to informal labour with no employment protections, often in the service sector. The state’s discriminatory policies have worsened their already precarious socio-economic conditions, solidifying existing barriers and institutionalizing discrimination in the labour sphere.’[footnote 260]

13.4.8 Equality Movement noted in a statement to the CGRS, made in July 2025 and published in the CGRS 2025 Report in September 2025: ‘Since the adoption of the anti-LGBT law, the social and economic exclusion of the LGBTQ+ community has alarmingly intensified. Local community organizations and service providers report incidents such as the dismissal of transgender individuals from workplaces on the basis of their gender identity…’[footnote 261]

13.4.9 Equality Movement noted in a further statement to the CGRS, made in September 2025 and equally published in the CGRS 2025 Report in the same month: ‘The “Law on Family Values and Minors” also significantly affects the community’s access to employment as it provides vaguely formulated provision on labor rights exempting employers from anti-discriminatory obligations to respect the person’s gender identity in labor relations …’[footnote 262]

13.4.10 Equality Movement continued in the same statement:

‘The cycle of socio-economic exclusion of the LGBTI community creates significant barriers to their access to the labor market. Studies indicate that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is widespread, occurring both during recruitment processes and throughout employment. In addition, a person’s sexual orientation and/or gender identity often serve as grounds for employment termination. Such barriers often compel LGBTI individuals to hide their identity in the workplace. Equality Movement’s internal “research on the updated needs of the LGBTQ+ community in relation to healthcare, psychosocial and legal services” reveal that for ‘open’ members of the community, the service industry—particularly its entertainment sector—remains the relatively feasible and safe space for employment. However, this sector is characterized by inadequate labor regulations, job instability, and low wages, which contribute significantly to the structural poverty experienced by the community. The cases of labour rights violations processed by Equality Movement’s lawyers frequently involve a person’s illegal dismissal from a work motivated by homophobia.’[footnote 263]

13.4.11 Equality Movement also noted in a statement to the CGRS that was published in the CGRS 2025 Report: ‘… employment opportunities are particularly limited for openly identified [LGBTI] community members. Even within the service industry, which is considered relatively more accessible, they are often subject to exotification—a practice that undermines, rather than supports, genuine emancipation.’[footnote 264]

13.4.12 The Council of Europe’s Group of Experts on Action against Trafficking in Human Beings noted in a report published in October 2025, that individuals of diverse SOGIE ‘…face difficulties in accessing the labour market, as employment opportunities are scarce for those who identify outside the traditional gender binary, leading them to work more in the informal economy (including prostitution) or even to accept abusive job offers.’[footnote 265]

14. Freedom of movement

14.1.1 The WISG 2025 Report observed: ‘… [C]oncerns around safety in public spaces have intensified. Increasingly, activists are avoiding preferred gathering locations and instead opting for alternative venues, choosing to use taxis rather than public transportation to minimize the risk of violence. These adaptations reveal how deeply security concerns are limiting the community’s freedom of movement …, compelling them to adopt restrictive survival strategies.’[footnote 266]
